data.title: Europe and Asia See Pickup in Activity Despite Headwinds — 3rd Update
data.description:
By Paul Hannon and Fabiana Negrin Ochoa

Business activity in the U.S., Europe and parts of Asia has picked up in the face of a series of headwinds related to the war in the Middle East, according to surveys released Friday.

A lack of progress on reopening the Strait of Hormuz or reaching a deal to end the nearly six-month war has kept energy prices high, while a rise in yields on government bonds is pushing up borrowing costs for households and businesses.

However, the surveys of purchasing managers suggested the global economy might avoid a further modest slowdown in the third quarter.

Although some major economies have yet to report, the available data suggests the global economy cooled slightly in the second quarter, led by the U.S. and China.

"While downside risks seem to be all around us, the economy remains stubbornly decent for the moment," Bert Colijn, an economist at ING, wrote in a note to clients.

S&P Global said its purchasing managers' index for the U.S.--which measures activity in the services and manufacturing sectors--rose to 56 in August from 54.5 in July.

"Business is booming, with firms reporting the fastest output growth for over four years," said Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence.

A reading below 50 points to a contraction, while a reading above that threshold points to an increase in activity.

With new orders remaining "robust," S&P said businesses reported a sharp increase in payrolls after little change over the previous eight months.

The PMI for the eurozone rose to 52.1 in August from 52.0 in July to reach its highest level in nine months.

The pickup was led by the German manufacturing sector, which saw its strongest growth since January 2022, and supported by increased demand for AI-related technology and military equipment.

France was once again the weakest part of the eurozone economy, recording another decline in activity.

The U.K. also recorded a pickup in activity, but one driven by the dominant services sector as manufacturing cooled. In Asia, there were accelerations in Japan and India.

But while growth strengthened, inflationary pressures eased. U.S. businesses reported the smallest increase in the prices they paid for inputs since the start of the war, while their counterparts in the eurozone and Asia also saw a cooling of costs.

They responded by raising their own prices less sharply. In the U.S., businesses reported the smallest increase since November, while their counterparts also trimmed hikes.

There were other signs that the impact of the war on global prices may be weaker than once feared.

A separate survey released by the European Central Bank on Friday found that in July, consumers expected inflation to be slightly lower over the coming 12 months than they did in June.

The central bank reported that wages negotiated by labor unions and similar groups rose at an annual rate of just 2.44% in the second quarter, a slowdown from 2.56% in the first.

However, the resilience displayed by leading economies might reassure some central banks that they can raise their key rates to contain inflation without risking too much harm to output and jobs.

The ECB is expected to increase borrowing costs next month, while Marcel Thieliant, an economist at Capital Economics, said the pickup in Japan strengthens the justification for the country's central bank to do likewise.

data.title: U.S. Business Activity Expands in August
data.description:
By Jessica Coacci

U.S. business activity in the private sector continued to expand this month, a monthly survey said.

The S&P Global Flash U.S. Composite PMI - based on its surveys of services and manufacturing firms, rose to 56 in August from 54.5 in July. A reading above 50 indicates activity continued to grow.

A surge in service sector business activity helped offset a marked slowing of growth in the manufacturing sector, the latter blamed in part on reduced inventory building and supply delays, the survey said.

"U.S. business is booming, with firms reporting the fastest output growth for over four years so far in the third quarter as the expansion picked up further momentum in August," said Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence.

Price pressures meanwhile moderated, especially in terms of selling price inflation. Input cost inflation remained elevated due to higher energy prices, the survey said.

data.title: Eurozone Consumer Sentiment Climbs to Highest Level Since February
data.description:
By Ed Frankl

Consumer sentiment in the eurozone unexpectedly edged higher for the fourth straight month in August, as the economy continues to show robust growth despite the energy-price shock from the Iran war.

The European Commission's flash eurozone consumer-confidence indicator published Friday rose to minus 15.5 from minus 15.9 in July. A consensus of economists polled last week by The Wall Street Journal expected it to fall a little to minus 16.2.

Despite the improving trend in recent months, consumer confidence hasn't yet recovered to the minus 12.4 of February before the outbreak of the conflict in the Middle East. The index remains below its long-term average, the commission said.

However, the rise in consumer sentiment tallies with business surveys also published Friday. Business activity accelerated a little this month, according to purchasing managers' index data. The eurozone's economy expanded by 0.4% in the second quarter of the year.

There was also an improvement in U.K. consumer confidence, which rose to its brightest level in two years, data published earlier Friday showed.

data.title: BJ's Wholesale Wins Value-Seeking Shoppers With Deals on Gas and Groceries — Update
data.description:
By Connor Hart

BJ's Wholesale Club raised its full-year profit outlook, as lower gas prices and deals on groceries drew more customers to its warehouses in the latest quarter.

"Gas prices are about as visible as it gets for consumers," Chief Executive Bob Eddy said on a call with analysts Friday. "There's a price on every street corner, and our members know that we offer great value."

Including fuel, comparable-club sales grew nearly 12% in the recent quarter. Stripping out fuel, comparable sales were up 3.1%, ahead of the 2.6% increase that analysts polled by FactSet expected.

The growth was driven by what Eddy called a healthy balance of traffic and ticket, with standout categories including grocery, consumer electronics and homegoods. BJ's notched growth across all income cohorts, though the majority was driven by higher-income households, as has been the case for the past several quarters, he added.

"In an environment where consumers remain discerning with their dollars, we know our job is to make sure we're putting the right products at the right value in front of every member who walks through our doors," Eddy said.

Shares rose 4.6% to $95.51 in morning trading. Despite the gain, the stock has lost roughly 10% of its value over the past year.

BJ's has received substantially all of the tariff refunds it expects, and the company has reinvested the majority of the money back into the company to lower prices, according to Eddy. He added that BJ's has additional initiatives in place to continue funding investments in price through the remainder of the year.

BJ's member count stood at a record 8.5 million as of Aug. 1. Membership-fee income rose 9.9% to $135.6 million during the quarter and helped drive total revenue 16% higher, to $6.23 billion.

The company posted a profit of $173.9 million, or $1.36 a share, up from $150.7 million, or $1.14 a share, a year earlier. Adjusted earnings were still $1.36 a share, ahead of Wall Street models for $1.17 a share

Looking ahead, BJ's said it now expects adjusted earnings of $4.60 to $4.80 a share for its current fiscal year, ending Jan. 30. That compares with a prior forecast of $4.40 to $4.60 a share. The company continues to project comparable-club sales, excluding the impact of gasoline sales, to be up 2% to 3%.

Analysts are looking for adjusted earnings of $4.53 a share and comparable-club sales growth of 2.5%.

By Anvee Bhutani

Arbutus Biopharma shares rose to a new 52-week high Friday after the clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company said it plans to repurchase up to $230 million of its common shares through a modified Dutch auction tender offer.

Shares were recently up 9.4% at $5.22.

The company expects to offer to buy shares at between $5.00 and $5.75 each, using cash on hand. The tender offer is expected to begin around Aug. 24 and expire around Sept. 29, unless extended or terminated.

Arbutus said the repurchase follows its March settlement with Moderna and a $200 million initial payment received in July under that settlement.

President and CEO Lindsay Androski said the company intends to return proceeds from the settlement to shareholders while continuing to enforce its rights against alleged infringers, including Pfizer and BioNTech.
